GOV.UK (MoD), published 26 Nov 2026 09:30 GMT



About the Strategic Reserve 

The Strategic Reserve is made up of some former Armed Forces personnel who have a legal liability to return to military service in a national emergency, an attack on the United Kingdom or a transition to war. Strategic Reservists are civilians unless they are formally called out or recalled. 

Most veterans do not have a Strategic Reserve liability. Having a liability does not mean that you are likely to be mobilised. 

The two parts of the Strategic Reserve 

The Ex-Regular Reserve includes former Service personnel who have an ongoing legal liability to train and, in times of great need, to be called out. 

The Recall Reserve includes former Service personnel who have an ongoing legal liability to be recalled in the most serious circumstances. 

Why Defence is contacting Strategic Reservists 

The United Kingdom faces a more dangerous and unpredictable security environment. Defence is re-engaging with the Strategic Reserve to: 

help people understand their legal liability 

improve contact and skills information 

offer some training and service opportunities 

test and improve mobilisation arrangements 

General contact from Defence, a request to update information, or an invitation to volunteer for training or service opportunities, is not a mobilisation notice. 

Strategic Reserve liability is not conscription 

Strategic Reserve liability arises from a person’s previous voluntary military service and the terms under which they served. It does not create a liability for the wider public. 

Your Strategic Reserve liability 

Factors that determine liability 

The nature and length of a person’s liability depend on their individual service. Relevant factors can include: 

Service 

rank 

whether service was in the Regular Forces or Volunteer Reserve 

dates and type of service 

the terms and conditions under which the person served 

Not every veteran has a liability. Liability does not mean a person will automatically be called out or recalled. 

Checking your liability 

Your Certificate of Service should record the position that applied when you left the Armed Forces. Defence is aware of errors affecting some people who left between 2006 and 2015. If your certificate is unclear or appears inconsistent with your service history, contact the relevant Service rather than relying on the certificate alone.

Keeping your information up to date 

When Defence provides an official route, keep your contact details, skills, qualifications and relevant personal information up to date. New civilian skills and experience may be relevant to future opportunities for training, service opportunities or mobilisation planning. 

Changes in personal circumstances 

A change in health, family circumstances or employment does not automatically remove a legal liability. If you receive a formal call out or recall notice and believe you cannot meet the requirement on a ground set out in law, the notice will explain how to ask for the decision to be reviewed. 

Living overseas 

A person may remain in the Strategic Reserve while living overseas. The position can depend on the country of residence and the nature of any employment for another nation. Contact the relevant Service for advice about individual circumstances. 

Training, service and mobilisation

Training and service opportunities 

Members of the Ex-Regular Reserve have a training liability that is rarely used at present. 

Defence is developing opportunities for suitable people to take part in training, exercises or service. Volunteering does not guarantee selection and is separate from compulsory mobilisation. 

When the Strategic Reserve could be used 

Call out and recall are legal processes used to return an eligible Strategic Reservist to military service. The legal route depends on the person’s reserve status and the circumstances. 

The threshold is high. The Strategic Reserve would not be used to fill routine staffing shortages in peacetime. It may be considered for serious national emergencies, warlike operations, preparations for war or a major crisis that requires additional military capability. 

How people would be selected 

Defence would match a requirement to suitable people. It may consider: 

military and civilian skills and qualifications 

time since leaving Service
